newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan sees little impact seen from refinery fire.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan sees little impact seen from refinery fire.

text.p: Taiwan state oil monopoly Chinese Petroleum Corp said on Friday that Thursday's fire at its Taoyuan refinery caused about T$20 million in damage, but would have no significant impact on production or supplies.
Executives nonetheless declined to give an estimate for when the affected refining unit would be brought back on line.
The fire and explosion struck on the very day that the hydro-desulfurisation unit was to have been restarted at the end of a routine maintenance shutdown of several weeks.
"Initial estimates show T$20 million in equipment losses," Chinese Petroleum said in a preliminary investigation report.

The late Thursday blaze struck one of the refinery's two hydro-desulfurisation units, which had been closed for annual maintenance since April 22 and had finished its scheduled checks on May 22 with no problems reported, the report said.
The affected unit has a capacity to process 15,000 tonnes of residual oil per month. The second hydro-desulfurisation unit at the plant can process 30,000 tonnes.
A Taoyuan refinery official said the accident would have little impact on Chinese Petroleum's supplies as only one unit was affected and it was the smaller of the two.
"The damaged unit is the smaller one and we almost never need to run at full capacity anyway," the official said. "Jet fuel and other product supplies will have no problem at all."

Some officials in the monopoly's Taipei office estimated on Thursday that the damaged unit's reopening would be delayed for up to a month, but declined when pressed on Friday to give any reopening date or estimate the value of any lost production.

The Taoyuan refinery has a monthly capacity of 60,000 tonnes of jet fuel, which mainly serves Taiwan's domestic market, is Chinese Petroleum's main production facility for jet fuel, supplying for the nearby Taipei international airport.
Investigators said they were trying to determine the cause of the initial fire, which triggered a series of hydrogen explosions in the hydro-desulfurisation unit, officials said.

The accident at Taoyuan was the second to hit Taiwan's oil giant on Thursday, coming just hours after a two-minute power outage in southern Kaohsiung that forced a costly shutdown of its huge No.5 naphtha cracker and a score of affiliated plants.
